name: Sound Detectives
subtitle: Aural skills and the elements of music
blurb: Ten weeks of listening. You build a toolkit for describing what you hear, use it on jazz, film music and Australian music, and learn to write about music with evidence.

cover.alt: A scruffy sketched crow in a detective hat, inspecting a music note through a magnifying glass

outcomes: uses listening skills to analyse music in relation to stylistic, cultural, historical and social contexts
uses listening skills to evaluate how the elements of music are manipulated and combined

assessment.name: AT3 Listening Examination
assessment.detail: Four excerpts and one extended response. 20 marks, worth 25%. Each excerpt mixes multiple choice and short answer parts with parts you write. The paper runs 40 minutes.

position.note: Lesson 8 ran Monday 10 August, Period 2. Next is Lesson 9: Writing about music, on Friday 14 August. Two lessons remain before the AT3 examination on Wednesday 19 August.

weeks.title: The Elements Toolkit
weeks.intro: Welcome to our listening unit. This week we meet the six elements of music and learn to describe what we hear in clear, musical language.

lessons.title: Active listening and the elements of music
lessons.intention: I can name the elements of music and use them to describe what I hear.
criteria: I can identify at least three elements in a short excerpt.
I can use the right word for each element.

blocks.brief: An engaging contemporary track to listen to first (teacher choice). Students just listen and jot what they notice.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Listen to the track and jot down anything you hear.
Meet the six elements of music: duration, pitch, texture, performing media & timbre, dynamics & expression, structure.
Fill in the elements table on this page as we meet each one.
Add each term to your listening glossary.
Listen again and tag what you hear to an element.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Everyone can hear music. Listening means hearing it in categories.

body.p: You can love a song for years and still not be able to say one useful thing about how it works. That is not a failure of taste, it is just that hearing and listening are different jobs. Hearing happens on its own. Listening is deliberate, and it is a skill you can get better at quickly.

The six elements are not a list to memorise. They are six questions you can ask of any piece of music ever written, and the trick is to ask **one at a time**. Trying to notice everything at once is how you end up noticing nothing. Play a track and listen only for texture, and you will hear things you have missed on fifty previous plays.
For the rest of this term, every excerpt gets the same six questions. The music changes every lesson. The questions never do.

blocks.title: The six elements
blocks.prompt: We fill this in together as we meet each one. Write what you listen for.

blocks.text: Make a list of every element you can hear in the track, with one word describing how it is used.
Name three elements you heard today.

teacher: Use the ‘Elements of Music’ deck to introduce the six elements.

lessons.title: Duration and pitch (listen and play)
lessons.intention: I can identify duration and pitch features by ear.
criteria: I can describe the tempo, metre and rhythm of an excerpt.
I can describe a melody’s shape (contour) and range.

blocks.text: How music moves through time: is it fast or slow, are the notes short or long, does it have a steady beat or does it feel off-kilter?
How high or low the notes are, and what the melody does: does it climb, fall, stay put?

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Beat, tempo, metre and rhythm are four different things, and only one of them is your foot.

body.p: These four get mixed up more than any other words in music, and it costs marks, because writing “the rhythm speeds up” when you mean the tempo speeds up tells the marker you cannot hear the difference. You do not separate them by memorising four definitions. You separate them by testing them against each other on a real track.

body.h: Four tests, on any track you like

ul: **Tap your foot.** What you are tapping is the beat. It keeps going underneath whether anyone plays a note on it or not.
**Count how quickly you are tapping.** That is the tempo.
**Notice that some taps feel stronger than others.** Strong, weak, weak. Strong, weak, weak. That grouping is the metre, and it is why some music feels like it is in threes and some in fours.
**Now follow the tune instead of your foot.** The pattern of long and short notes in the tune is the rhythm, and it almost never lines up exactly with your tapping. That mismatch is the point of it.

body.p: **Working rule: tempo and rhythm are independent.** Play the same rhythm twice as fast and it is still the same rhythm, just quicker. If you can change one without touching the other, they are not the same thing, and these are the two students collapse into one most often.

body.h: Pitch: describe the motion, not the notes

body.p: Nobody is asking you to name notes by ear. You are being asked to describe movement. A melody's **contour** is its shape over time, whether it climbs, falls, arches or waves. Its **range** is how far it reaches from its lowest note to its highest, which is a separate question: a melody can have a dramatic shape inside a narrow range, or barely move across a wide one. When it moves a small distance to the next note it has stepped, and when it jumps a long way it has leapt. Shape, distance, and how far the whole thing spans. That is the level of detail a listening answer wants.

blocks.title: Duration words
blocks.prompt: We fill these in together. Write what each one means.

blocks.title: Tempo words (Italian)
blocks.prompt: Same again. These are the words on the score that tell you the speed.

blocks.title: Pitch words
blocks.prompt: And the pitch half of the lesson.

blocks.brief: A short rhythmic example (clear beat and metre) and a short melodic example (clear melody) , one of each.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Recap: duration = beat, tempo, metre, rhythm. Pitch = melody, contour, range.
Write the definitions of duration and pitch in your books.
Fill in the duration, tempo and pitch tables on this page as we work through them.
Clap or play the rhythm patterns as a class.
Play or sing the short melodies and describe their shape.
Listen and identify these features by ear.

blocks.text: Notate or describe a 4-bar rhythm you hear, then describe the contour of a short melody (rising, falling, wave).
Was the melody’s range wide or narrow? How do you know?

lessons.title: Writing about music 1
lessons.intention: I can write a clear sentence about how an element is used.
criteria: My sentence names the element.
It says how the element is used and its effect, with evidence.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Name it, say how it is used, say what it does, say where you heard it.

body.p: Writing about music is not writing about how the music made you feel. It is evidence. Every point you make has four parts, and a sentence missing one of them is usually the reason an answer scores lower than the student expected.

ul: **Name** the element you are writing about.
**How it is used** - what you actually hear, in enough detail that the marker can hear it too.
**Effect** - what that does to the music or to the listener. This is the part people leave out.
**Evidence** - where in the music it happens.

body.p: You will meet this again in Lesson 9 with a fully worked example and a marked-out zero-mark answer. For now, get all four parts into every sentence you write, and check your partner's for the one they dropped.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Learn the response sentence: element + how it is used + effect + evidence.
Build a class response to a short excerpt together.
Write one paragraph on your own.
Swap with a partner and check against the sentence frame.

blocks.text: Write one paragraph about a short excerpt using the sentence frame for at least two elements.
Underline the ‘effect’ part of your best sentence.

teacher: Model the sentence on the board: element + how it is used + effect + musical evidence. Build one together before students write.

weeks.title: Texture, Timbre and Comparing
weeks.intro: This week we listen across styles to explore texture and timbre, and learn how to compare two works using the elements of music.

lessons.title: Texture across styles (listen and build)
lessons.intention: I can identify and describe texture in different styles.
criteria: I can name the texture type (monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic).
I can explain how the layers combine.

blocks.text: The way layers of sound are combined in a piece of music.

blocks.brief: Suggestions: Gregorian chant (search ‘Gregorian chant Kyrie’), or unaccompanied solo voice/instrument.

blocks.text: A single melodic line with no accompaniment.

blocks.brief: Suggestions: a simple pop or hymn arrangement (e.g. a band playing melody over strummed/block chords), or a piano/vocal ballad.

blocks.text: A melody with chordal accompaniment.

blocks.brief: Suggestions: a Bach fugue (e.g. ‘Little Fugue in G minor’), a round/canon (e.g. ‘Frère Jacques’ sung in canon), or a jazz combo with independent improvised lines.

blocks.text: Two or more independent melodic lines combined.

blocks.title: More texture words
blocks.prompt: The three texture types are defined above. These are the other words we use about layers.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Read the texture definition and each texture type.
Listen to the excerpt after each definition and check it matches.
Fill in the texture words table on this page as we listen.
In groups, build a texture by adding one layer at a time.
Describe how the texture changed as layers were added.

blocks.text: For each excerpt, name the texture type and explain how the layers combine to create it.
Which excerpt had the thickest texture, and why?

teacher: Use the ‘Elements of Music’ deck (texture section) for the diagrams.

lessons.title: Performing media and timbre
lessons.intention: I can identify performing media and describe timbre.
criteria: I can name the instruments or voices I hear.
I can describe their tone colour using musical words.

blocks.text: What's making the sound, and what it actually sounds like — an instrument's ‘personality’.

blocks.title: Performing media words
blocks.prompt: We fill these in together. Write what each one means.

blocks.title: Instrument families
blocks.prompt: Different job: name one instrument you heard from each family.

blocks.brief: World: a raga on solo sitar — a distinctive, sustained plucked-string timbre.
Jazz: Louis Armstrong's gravelly vocal timbre, instantly recognisable — this famous recording has no trumpet on it, just his voice against strings.
Film: the Star Wars Main Title, full orchestral timbre.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Recap: performing media = the sound sources; timbre = their tone colour.
Listen and build a class ‘timbre word bank’ (bright, warm, harsh, mellow, etc.).
Fill in the performing media and instrument family tables on this page as we go.
Play an instrument ID quiz with short clips.
Match a timbre word to each instrument you hear.

blocks.text: For each clip, name the instruments or voices and give one word for their tone colour.
Pick one instrument and describe its timbre in a full sentence.

teacher: Use the ‘Elements of Music’ deck (timbre section).

lessons.title: Comparing 'Valerie'
lessons.intention: I can compare two versions of the same song using performing media and timbre.
criteria: I can name the voices and instruments I hear in each version.
I can describe the tone colour of each one using musical words.
I can write one similarity and one difference, and back each up with musical evidence.

blocks.text: The voices and instruments used to perform a piece of music — in other words, what is making the sound.

The quality of a sound that makes one voice or instrument sound different from another, even when they play exactly the same note. A trumpet and a flute playing the same pitch do not sound the same, and timbre is the word for that difference.

blocks.brief: Version A: The Zutons, 2006 — the original.
Version B: Mark Ronson featuring Amy Winehouse, 2007 — same melody, words and chords, completely different performing media and timbre.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Copy both definitions into your book, and the timbre word bank.
Listen once through to each version without writing anything: who is singing, what carries the hook, what holds the rhythm, what sits on top.
Listen again and rule up a table in your book: the voice, the instrument that leads, the rhythm section, anything else you can hear, and three tone-colour words for each version.
Every comparison point needs three parts: name it, give the evidence you heard, and explain the effect.

blocks.text: Write one similarity and one difference between the two versions, each backed with musical evidence and its effect. Performing media and timbre are marked together as one 2-mark question in the listening exam — naming the instruments alone only gets you one mark, you need the tone-colour description too.
Which version's tone colour suits the song better, and why? Name at least one voice or instrument in your answer.

weeks.title: Dynamics, Structure and Exam Writing
weeks.intro: This week we finish the toolkit with dynamics, expression and structure, and start writing full responses to the exam question.

lessons.title: Dynamics and expression
lessons.intention: I can identify dynamics and expression and explain their effect.
criteria: I can describe how the volume changes.
I can explain how a change in dynamics changes the mood.

blocks.text: How loud or soft the music is, and the little performance tricks (sliding, plucking, shaking a note) that add feeling.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: A dynamic level is a fact. A dynamic change is an answer.

body.p: Most students write “the music is loud” and stop, which describes one second of a piece and earns nothing. Dynamics is not really about volume. It is about the shape volume makes across time, and what that shape does to you.

body.h: Three things to listen for, in order of what they are worth

ul: **The level.** Loud or soft, right now. Worth naming, worth nothing on its own.
**The change.** Does it grow or fall away, and does it do it suddenly or gradually? This is where the marks start, because you can only hear it by listening across time rather than at one moment.
**The effect.** What that change does to the music and to the listener. This is where the marks actually are.

body.p: **Working rule: if you could answer it by reading one word off the score, it is not analysis yet.** Anyone can see _forte_ written on a page. Only someone listening can tell you whether the music arrived there in one step or crept up on you over ninety seconds, and those two do completely different things to a listener.

body.h: Expression is how a note is played, not how loud it is

body.p: Two players can play the same note, at the same volume, at the same moment, and sound nothing alike. One plays it smooth and joined to the next note, the other cuts it short. One leans on it, the other slides into it from underneath. One shakes the note, the other holds it dead still. That is expression, and it is usually what makes a style instantly recognisable: the same melody played with the articulation of one style and then another stops sounding like the same music at all.

blocks.title: Dynamics words
blocks.prompt: We fill these in together. Type the English meaning next to each term.

blocks.title: Expression words
blocks.prompt: Same again. These are the performance details that give a style its feel.

blocks.brief: A film music cue with clear dynamic changes (quiet build to a loud climax).

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Recap: dynamics = volume; expression = the detail that gives a style its feel (articulation, accents).
Listen to the film cue and follow a listening map of the dynamics.
Mark where the music gets louder or softer and what happens to the mood.
Fill in the dynamics and expression tables on this page as we work through them.
Add expression words (legato, staccato, accent) to your glossary.

blocks.text: On a listening map, track the dynamics of the cue and write one sentence on how a change in dynamics changed the mood.
Name one moment where dynamics created tension.

teacher: Use the ‘Elements of Music’ deck (dynamics & expression section).

lessons.title: Structure
lessons.intention: I can identify the structure of a work by ear.
criteria: I can label the sections of a work.
I can describe how the sections differ.

blocks.text: How the piece is put together — the order of its sections, like the shape of a story.

blocks.call: Structure is the only element you cannot hear in a single moment.

body.p: Every other element is there in one second of sound. You can hear that a note is high, that a chord is loud, that a tone is brassy, without waiting for anything. Structure is different. It only exists across time: it is the pattern you notice when you compare what you are hearing now with what you heard a minute ago.
A new section almost never announces itself with one change. It arrives with two or three at once. The usual ones:

ul: instruments come in, or drop out (texture)
the music gets louder or softer (dynamics)
the drum pattern changes, or the beat drops out altogether
the melody changes, or an earlier melody comes back
the words change, or earlier words come back
the harmony moves somewhere it has not been

body.p: **Working rule: if two or more of those change at the same moment, that moment is a boundary.** If only one changes, it is usually decoration inside a section rather than the start of a new one.
You cannot be certain a section was a chorus until it comes back, which is exactly why you get three playings in a listening examination. Use the first playing to notice, and the later ones to label.
Use letters (A, B, A) when the sections have no names, and names (intro, verse, chorus, bridge, outro) when they do. Either way you are drawing a map: the sections in order, left to right.

blocks.label: Excerpt 1
blocks.brief: A pop song with a clear verse-chorus structure. Follow one thing all the way through: the words “Lately I’ve been”. Count how many times they come back.

cues.text: The song opens with its chorus, over an acoustic guitar and almost nothing else. Remember this tune. You will hear it four more times.
The band arrives: bass, kit, handclaps. The tune has not changed, the texture has. A boundary can be carried by texture on its own.
Verse 1. New words, new melody, and the drums settle into a pattern they keep. Two changes at once, so this boundary is unmistakable.
Chorus 1. The tune from 0:00, now with the full band behind it. Same tune, different dress, which is how you know 0:00 was the chorus.
Bridge. Everything drops away except the voice and a few chords, and one short phrase repeats four times. This is the biggest change in the song, and the only section that happens once.

blocks.text: The pop-song structure: verses tell the story, the chorus is the hook that repeats.

blocks.label: Excerpt 2
blocks.work: Stevie Ray Vaughan & Double Trouble, “Pride and Joy”
blocks.brief: A 12-bar blues. Nothing here is a verse or a chorus in the pop sense. The whole track is one 12-bar pattern, played through nine times without changing shape once.

cues.text: The riff, on guitar alone. It is the engine of the whole song and it barely stops for three and a half minutes.
Bass and drums join. From here you can count: four beats to a bar, at about 127 beats a minute.
The first 12 bars begin. In blues, one trip through the 12 bars is called a _chorus_, whether anyone sings on it or not. It is a unit of form, not a hook.
Chorus 3. Follow the chords all the way through this one.

sub.text: Bars 1 to 4, all on the home chord (I).
Bar 5. The chord steps up to IV. This is the moment that proves it is a 12-bar blues and not just a repeat.
Bar 9. Up to V, the furthest from home the pattern ever goes.
Bars 11 and 12. Home to I, and a turnaround that hands you back to bar 1.

cues.text: Chorus 5, and the guitar takes a solo. The form does not bend for it: the solo fits inside the same 12 bars as everything else.
The ending. The band steps outside the pattern for the first time in the whole song, and stops on the home chord.

blocks.note: Each chorus runs about 22 and a half seconds. Time the gap between any two of the boundaries above and you get the same number, which is what “the form repeats unchanged” actually means when you measure it.

blocks.text: A repeating 12-bar chord pattern, often with an AAB lyric pattern — the backbone of blues and early rock 'n' roll.

blocks.label: Excerpt 3
blocks.work: Mozart, 12 Variations on “Ah, vous dirai-je, maman”, K. 265
blocks.brief: Two forms on one track. The theme has a ternary (ABA) shape of its own, and the set then rebuilds that theme twelve times in different clothes. You already know the tune.

cues.text: The theme. Listen to its own shape first, before any variation starts.

sub.text: **A again**, note for note. Composers repeat before they contrast.
**B.** A new middle idea, higher, stepping downwards.
**A returns**, unchanged. A, then B, then A: that is ternary form, sitting inside the theme.
B and A again, because this half of the theme is repeated too.

cues.text: **Variation 8.** The one everybody notices. Same tune, same shape, same number of bars, in a _minor_ key. Nothing structural changed. Only the colour did.

blocks.note: Every variation has the same number of bars and the same chords underneath as the theme. What changes is speed, register, which hand has the fast notes, how much decoration, major or minor, and finally the metre. In other words, every element _except_ structure. That is what a variation is.

blocks.text: Ternary (ABA): a section, a contrasting middle, then a return to the start. Theme and variation: one melody, dressed up differently each time it repeats.

blocks.title: Structure words
blocks.prompt: The forms are defined above. These are the section names we use inside them.

blocks.summary: If you were away: the structure words
items: **Intro** - the opening section that sets the song up before the singing starts.
**Verse** - carries the story. Same tune each time, new words each time.
**Pre-chorus** - a short section between verse and chorus that builds tension and hands over.
**Chorus** - repeats with the same words and the same tune. Usually the loudest, and the one you remember.
**Bridge** - appears once, usually late, and contrasts with everything around it.
**Instrumental (solo)** - no singing, an instrument takes the lead line.
**Outro (coda)** - the ending section, after the last chorus.
**Riff** - a short pattern, usually on guitar, bass or keys, repeated as the backbone of a section.
**Hook** - the part you cannot stop singing. Often the chorus line, but it can be a riff.
**Repetition** - using the same material again. It is what makes a section recognisable when it returns.
**Contrast** - putting something different beside it. It is what makes a boundary audible in the first place.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Recap forms: verse-chorus, 12-bar blues, ternary (ABA), theme and variation.
Listen and map the sections of each excerpt.
Fill in the structure words table on this page as we map each excerpt.
Discuss what tells you a new section has started (a change in an element).
Compare how the three structures are organised.

blocks.text: Map the structure of one excerpt by labelling its sections and noting what changes between them.

blocks.question: Describe one thing that changes when a new section begins.
blocks.lead: This is the question type your listening examination asks about structure, and it is this lesson’s exit question in the same words. Here is one full mark, on “Counting Stars”.
blocks.model: At 3:26 the full band returns after the bridge, so the texture thickens from one voice and a few chords to drums, bass and guitars all at once, and that thickening is what marks the start of the final chorus.

rungs.text: Name the change and say where it is. _The texture thickens at 3:26._ “The texture changes” on its own names an element but not a change, and earns nothing.
Add the sound and the location. _From one voice and a few chords to drums, bass and guitars._ The marker should be able to hear it from your words without playing the track.
Say what it does. _That thickening marks the start of the final chorus._ This is the half the question is really paying for, and the half most people leave off.

zero.why: True, and worth zero: it says a section changed without saying what changed. The mark is for the hearing, not for the word count, so a short answer is fine. An empty one is not.

blocks.text: What element signalled a new section most clearly?

blocks.summary: Check yourself: four questions on today
items: In “Counting Stars”, which section appears only once? **The bridge, at 3:00.** Everything else comes round at least twice.
How long is one chorus of “Pride and Joy”, in seconds? **About 22 and a half.** Anything from 21 to 24 means you counted rather than guessed.
In Mozart’s Variation 8, what changed and what stayed the same? **The mode changed to minor. The tune, its length and its ABA shape stayed the same.**

Name two things that usually change together at a section boundary. **Any two of: texture, dynamics, drum pattern, melody, words, harmony.** One change on its own is usually decoration; two together is a boundary.

teacher: Use the ‘Elements of Music’ deck (structure section).

lessons.title: Writing about music: the response frame and the exam question
lessons.intention: I can write a full response on how the elements of music are used.
criteria: I can write a sentence that names an element, says how it is used, explains its effect and gives evidence.
I can write a full response covering three elements.

blocks.text: Every point you write about music has four parts: name the element, say how it is used, explain its effect, and give the musical evidence you actually heard. Miss the effect and you are describing, not analysing.

blocks.call: Every mark in this exam is earned by the word after “because”.

body.p: A response sentence has four parts: name the element, say how it is used, say what effect that has, and give the musical evidence you actually heard. Miss the effect and you have described the music, not analysed it. Description on its own earns nothing in this exam.

ul: **Name** - which element you are writing about (dynamics, structure, timbre, and so on).
**How it is used** - what you actually hear, in enough detail that the marker can hear it too.
**Effect** - what that does: to the mood, to the listener, to the piece. This is the “because”.
**Evidence** - where in the music it happens. A timestamp is evidence. So is “throughout”, if it is true.

body.p: **Working rule: if your sentence would still be true with the effect deleted, you have not written the effect.** “The dynamics get louder” survives without a because. “The dynamics get louder, which builds tension toward the chorus” does not. Delete the second half and the sentence falls over. That is the test.

ul: **Describing (no marks):** “The orchestra plays softly under the voice.” True, and it stops at naming what happens.

**Analysing (full marks):** “The orchestra plays softly under the voice, which lets the rough, worn quality of the voice come through instead of being covered by the sound around it.” Same observation, with the because attached.

body.p: The exam question is always some version of _how are the elements of music used to create interest?_ Part B is worth 6 of the 20 marks, so a full response covers three elements, one sentence like the ones above for each.

blocks.brief: A work we have already analysed, so that the writing is the new part, not the listening: Louis Armstrong, 'What a Wonderful World'.

blocks.question: How are the elements of music used to create interest?
blocks.marks: 2 of 6 marks - one paragraph of three
blocks.lead: This models one of your three paragraphs: timbre, on “What a Wonderful World”. The other two are yours to write, the same four-part shape, applied to whatever you actually hear.
blocks.model: Armstrong sings the whole track in his rough, gravelly voice, set against a smooth orchestra of strings, and that contrast in tone colour is what gives the song its warmth: a worn, human voice sitting over something polished and safe makes the song feel spoken to you rather than performed at you.

rungs.text: Say which element. _Timbre._ Naming it and stopping is where the zero answer below goes wrong.
Say what you actually hear, in contrast. _Armstrong’s rough, gravelly voice against a smooth string orchestra._ Two tone colours named against each other, not one word like “orchestra” on its own.

Say what that contrast does. _It makes the song feel warm and personal, like it is being spoken rather than performed._ This is the half of the sentence most people leave off, and the half that earns the mark.

Ground it in the music. _Throughout the track, and the voice never changes character against the strings._ Evidence does not have to be a timestamp. Something being true for the whole piece is evidence too.

zero.why: True, and worth nothing: it names the element and stops. No sound has been described, no effect has been claimed, nothing has been heard. It is the same shape as the zero-mark answer to structure in Lesson 8: naming an element is not analysing it.

items: Which part of the response sentence is most often left out? **The effect.** A sentence that only says what happens is describing, not analysing.
Is “the song uses dynamics” worth any marks on its own? **No.** It names the element and stops, with no description, no effect, no evidence.
What is the working rule for spotting a missing effect? **Delete the second half of the sentence. If it still stands up on its own, the effect was never there.**
How many elements does a full response need, going by this lesson’s exam question? **Three - one paragraph each, one sentence shape repeated three times.**

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Learn the response sentence: name, how it is used, effect, evidence.
Read the worked timbre paragraph and see the four parts at work.
Meet the exam question: how are the elements of music used to create interest?
Plan your own response: three elements, one paragraph each.
Write a full response and check each paragraph against the four parts.
Swap with a partner and underline the effect in each other's paragraphs.

blocks.text: Write a full response to the excerpt answering: how are the elements of music used to create interest? Cover three elements, one paragraph each. This is exactly the shape of Part B of the exam, which is worth 6 of the 20 marks.
Underline the 'effect' part of each of your three paragraphs.

teacher: The response sentence was introduced on the page in Lesson 3. This lesson is the full version: the four parts, a worked paragraph and a zero-mark answer. It is the shape every answer in the exam wants.
A full response is modelled on the board before you write your own.

weeks.title: Exam Preparation
weeks.intro: One lesson this week, because the trial examinations compress the class to two periods and the AT3 examination follows on Wednesday of Week 5. We rehearse the whole exam in a single period: listening widely, annotating as we listen, and writing a full response under time.

lessons.title: Exam preparation: wide listening, strategies and a timed response
lessons.intention: I can use exam strategies and write to the standard of the AT3 task.
criteria: I can identify the style and two elements of an excerpt quickly.
I can annotate an excerpt as I listen.
I can plan and write a full response under time pressure.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Quick-fire listening: three short excerpts, style plus two elements for each.
Meet the exam format: multiple choice and short answer parts as well as parts you write, 40 minutes for the whole paper.
Learn the three-playing strategy for the unseen excerpt.
Annotate the final excerpt in real time as it plays, three times, exactly as the exam runs.
Read the worked response, then plan and write your own.
Read the feedback and the common misconceptions before Wednesday.

blocks.label: Exam strategy
blocks.call: You get the unseen excerpt three times. Each playing has one job.

body.p: The paper gives you three playings of the unseen excerpt and forty minutes for the whole thing, so the playings are not three chances to catch what you missed - they are three different jobs, and doing the wrong job on the wrong playing is where marks go missing.

ul: **Playing 1** - answer the multiple choice and short answer questions. These ask for a fact (an element, a term, a feature) and reward speed, so get them down while the excerpt is fresh and leave the writing alone.
**Playing 2** - annotate. Jot the elements as you hear them, in your own shorthand, against roughly where they happen. This is raw material, not sentences.
**Playing 3** - check what you missed, and start turning your strongest annotations into the four-part response sentence from Lesson 9: name, how it is used, effect, evidence.

body.p: **Working rule: write nothing in full sentences until playing 3.** A response written during playing 1 or 2 is usually a description with the effect missing, because you were still listening for the next thing rather than thinking about what the last thing did.

You cannot write full sentences while the excerpt is running, so annotation is shorthand: an element's initial, an arrow for a change, a rough time. “D getting louder ~1:40” is a complete annotation. It is not a response sentence yet, but it has everything a response sentence needs, and that is the point of doing it in two steps rather than one.

blocks.brief: Quick-fire, world: Gamelan gong kebyar, 'Kapi Raja'. A distinctive percussive, metallic ensemble.
Quick-fire, classical: Vivaldi, Spring (The Four Seasons). Energetic Baroque strings.
Quick-fire, jazz: Take Five, the Dave Brubeck Quartet. An odd 5/4 metre.

blocks.label: Timed response excerpt
blocks.work: Grieg, “In the Hall of the Mountain King” (Peer Gynt)
blocks.brief: Unseen, and short enough to annotate start to finish. Tempo, dynamics and texture all build together here, which is exactly the kind of change the exam rewards you for catching. Play it three times, exactly as the exam runs: facts first, annotate second, write third.

cues.text: The ostinato theme begins low in the strings, pizzicato, very quiet and slow. Everything that happens for the next minute and a half is this same idea, gradually speeding up and growing louder.

No new instrument has entered and no section has changed, but the theme is already audibly faster and louder than at 0:00. This is the trap: there is no boundary to catch here, because the composer is building continuously rather than stepping between sections. Annotate it as a gradual change, not an event.

The one genuinely sudden moment in the piece: the full orchestra enters fortissimo, brass and all, at the fastest tempo yet. After ninety seconds of gradual build, this is the payoff, and it is unmistakable even on a first playing.
A grand pause. The orchestra drops to complete silence for a beat, the only silence in the whole excerpt.

sub.text: The silence is answered immediately by the loudest, fastest chords in the piece, driving straight to the end. Silence followed by the loudest possible re-entry is itself a dynamics device, worth naming on its own.

blocks.note: Measured off this exact recording, not recalled: the build from 0:00 to 1:42 is a continuous rise with no internal step, which is why it is described here as gradual rather than given a false halfway boundary. The piece runs out shortly after 2:51, the last thirty seconds of the three-minute file being trailing silence.

blocks.question: How are the elements of music used to create interest?
blocks.marks: 2 of 6 marks - one paragraph of three
blocks.lead: This models one paragraph on the Grieg, using dynamics rather than Lesson 9's timbre. The shape is identical: name, how it is used, effect, evidence.
blocks.model: Grieg builds the dynamics from a very quiet opening to a sudden fortissimo climax at 1:42, without ever stepping the volume up in stages, and that unbroken, gradual crescendo is what makes the eventual fortissimo feel inevitable rather than sudden: by the time the full orchestra enters, the listener has been pulled toward it for ninety seconds without a single break to relax into.

rungs.text: Say what you actually hear. _A continuous, unbroken crescendo from very quiet to fortissimo, with no stepped stages._ “It gets louder” is not enough detail on its own; continuous versus stepped is the detail that earns the mark.
Say what that does. _It makes the climax feel inevitable and pulls the listener toward it, rather than surprising them with a sudden change._
Ground it in the music. _The build runs from 0:00 to the fortissimo entry at 1:42, with the grand pause at 2:21 used as a second, sharper example of the same device._

zero.why: True, and it is describing, not analysing: it names the element and reports what happens, with no effect and no timed evidence attached. It is the same shape as the zero-mark timbre answer in Lesson 9.

items: What should you write during playing 1? **Nothing but the multiple choice and short answer questions.** Full sentences come later.

What is an annotation, and how is it different from a response sentence? **Shorthand jotted while listening** - an element, a change, a rough time. A response sentence is the four-part version you write afterwards from that shorthand.

Why does the Grieg excerpt's build from 0:00 to 1:42 resist being annotated as a single boundary? **Because it is continuous, not stepped** - nothing new enters, the change is gradual, so marking one moment as “the change” misrepresents what is actually happening.
What two things happen back to back at 2:21? **A grand pause (total silence), immediately answered by the loudest, fastest chords in the piece.**

blocks.text: Annotate the final excerpt as it plays, then write a full timed response to it: three elements, one paragraph each, under exam conditions.
Write down your personal exam plan in one sentence.

teacher: Bring your listening glossary and terminology bank. You get the strategy checklist at the start of the lesson.
The timed response runs under exam conditions, with the excerpt played three times and reading and writing time between playings, so Wednesday holds no surprises.
Performing media and timbre are still worth 2 marks together in the exam, but Canvas shows them as two separate questions. Nothing about that changes how you answer.

weeks.title: Jazz
weeks.intro: This week we listen to jazz, play a 12-bar blues and improvise, then analyse how jazz uses the elements of music to create interest.

lessons.title: Jazz listening
lessons.intention: I can identify the features and context of jazz.
criteria: I can name three features of jazz.
I can hear where improvisation happens.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Nobody wrote the solo down. That is the whole point, and you can hear it once you know what to listen for.

body.p: Jazz grew out of African American communities in the southern United States around the turn of the twentieth century, with New Orleans as its best-known starting point and the blues and ragtime as its roots. From there it spread through the dance bands of the 1930s and 40s and then into the small, fast, virtuosic groups of bebop. What holds all of that together is one habit: part of the music is invented while it is being played.

body.h: Four things that make it sound like jazz

ul: **Swing.** The beat is divided unevenly, long then short, instead of into equal halves. It is the difference between music you march to and music you nod to, and it is felt rather than notated.
**Improvisation.** Parts are made up in performance over an agreed chord pattern. Not random: the form and the chords are fixed and everyone is counting. Only the notes on top are free.

**Blue notes.** Certain notes are flattened or bent slightly below where a major scale would put them. That deliberate sourness against the chord underneath is where a lot of the ache in the sound comes from.

**The instrumentation.** A rhythm section (piano or guitar, bass, drums) holds the form steady, while a front line (trumpet, saxophone, trombone, or a voice) takes turns on top. Listen for that split and the rest gets easier to follow.

body.p: **How to tell an improvised section from a written one, which is your exit question:** written ensemble passages have everyone locked together, arriving and stopping at the same instant, as in the Glenn Miller. When a solo starts, the texture thins to one voice on top while the rhythm section keeps doing exactly what it was already doing. Solo phrases start and end in awkward places, breathe unevenly, and would come out different if the band played the tune again tomorrow.

blocks.brief: Vocal/standard: Ella Fitzgerald & Louis Armstrong, 'Summertime' — the classic jazz-standard vocal duo sound.
Big band: Glenn Miller, 'In the Mood' — the archetypal swing-era big band riff and ensemble sound.
Small-combo bebop: Charlie Parker, 'Ornithology' (1946) — fast bebop with an audible improvised alto solo.

lessons.title: Jazz practical: 12-bar blues
lessons.intention: I can perform and improvise within a 12-bar blues.
criteria: I can keep my place in the 12-bar form.
I can play a short improvised idea.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Twelve bars, three chords, and everybody arrives back at the top together.

body.p: The 12-bar blues is a fixed pattern of twelve bars that repeats for the length of the song. It is the reason musicians who have never met can play together for ten minutes without discussing anything first: once everyone knows where they are in the twelve, the rest looks after itself. You heard this pattern run nine times without changing in Lesson 8.

ul: **Bars 1 to 4** - I, the home chord.
**Bars 5 and 6** - IV.
**Bars 7 and 8** - back to I.
**Bar 9** - V, the furthest the pattern ever gets from home.
**Bars 11 and 12** - home to I, then a turnaround that hands you back to bar 1.

body.p: The numbers work in any key. In A, the most common classroom blues key, I is A7, IV is D7 and V is E7. Learn the pattern by its numbers rather than its chord names and you can move it to any key you are asked for.

ul: **Chords** - change on the right bar, not when it sounds like time. Count in fours the whole way through.
**Bass** - the root note of whichever chord is current, steady, no decoration needed.
**Rhythm and drums** - do not change with the chords. Your job is that the groove never wavers.
**Melody and solos** - use the blues scale, and aim to land somewhere sensible by bar 12.

body.p: **Working rule: the form does not stop for your solo.** The twelve bars keep turning underneath whether you play a note or not, so keep counting while you improvise. Coming back in at the wrong bar is the only real way to get lost in a blues.

blocks.brief: 12-bar blues backing track in A major, 100 bpm — a comfortable tempo for the class to play along with and improvise over.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Learn the 12-bar blues chord pattern.

weeks.title: Film Music
weeks.intro: This week we explore how film music creates mood and tells stories, create a short cue, and analyse a film composer’s choices.

lessons.title: Film music listening
lessons.intention: I can identify how film music supports narrative.
criteria: I can link a musical feature to an emotion or scene.
I can use the term leitmotif correctly.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Film music is not there to be noticed. It is there to tell you how to feel about what you are looking at.

body.p: Cut the same shot of someone walking down a corridor to three different pieces of music and you get three different scenes: a thriller, a comedy, a farewell. Nothing on screen changed. That is the whole job, and it means every choice in a film score is answerable to something happening in the story.

ul: **Leitmotif.** A short musical idea attached to a character, a place or an idea, brought back whenever they are relevant, and often altered to show what has happened to them since. Borrowed from opera and standard in film ever since.
**Underscore.** Music running under dialogue or action, deliberately kept out of the way. If you consciously noticed it during the film, it was probably doing its job badly.

**Mickey-mousing.** Music matching the action moment for moment, a musical gesture per footstep or per pratfall. Named after the cartoons that made it famous. Obvious, and usually comic when used in live action.

body.p: **Working rule: name the feature and the moment it serves.** “The music is tense” is not analysis, because it describes your reaction rather than the music. “The strings move to a fast tremolo as the door opens, which turns an ordinary action into a threat” names what the composer did, when, and what it bought them. That is the same four-part sentence from Lesson 3, pointed at a screen.

Be careful with rules like “minor key means sad”. They hold often enough to be worth knowing and are broken constantly by good composers. Describe what you actually hear in this cue, not what the textbook says the key should mean.

lessons.title: Critical listening: evaluating choices
lessons.intention: I can evaluate interpretive choices in performance.
criteria: I can compare two versions of a work.
I can justify a preference with musical evidence.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Evaluate means make a judgement and defend it. Liking one better is not a judgement.

body.p: Every listening task so far has asked you to **analyse**: how is this music put together, and what does that do. This one asks you to **evaluate**, which is a step up. You have to commit to a verdict about which interpretation works better, and then make someone else agree with you using nothing but the music.

body.h: What an evaluation has that an analysis does not

ul: **A judgement you commit to.** Not “both are good in their own way”. Pick one. Sitting on the fence reads as not having heard a difference.

**A stated criterion.** More effective _at what_? Building tension, carrying the words, suiting the venue, serving the composer's marking. You have to say, because that is the standard you are judging against.
**Evidence, same as always.** The tempo, dynamics, expression or timbre choice that actually made the difference.

body.p: **Working rule: name your criterion or the judgement is just taste.** Two performances of the same work are not better or worse in the abstract, and a marker cannot give credit for a preference. One is more effective _at_ something, and the moment you name that something, the evidence you need becomes obvious.
